Authors: Chien, S.-C.; Chien, C.-H.; Chen, C.-Y.; ... Li, Y.-C.
Source: Using technology acceptance model to explore physicians’ perspectives of clinical decision support system alerts
Abstract: Objective To examine factors influencing physicians’ perspectives of clinical decision support system (CDSS) alerts using the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), focusing on perceived ease of use (PEOU), perceived usefulness (PU), attitude towards usage (AT), user satisfaction (US) and behavioural intention to use (BI). Methods This study was conducted in the outpatient departments of a single academic medical centre in northern Taiwan, involving 72 physicians who completed a structured TAM-based questionnaire. Seven physician’s characteristics (age, clinical experience, CDSS operating status, patient volume, consultation frequency, gender and specialty) were analysed for their influence on PEOU and PU. Multiple regression analysis assessed relationships among TAM constructs and external factors. Results Patient volume and age negatively affected PU and PEOU (eg, age vs PU: β=−2.38, p<0.05; patient volume vs PEOU: β=−2.64, p<0.01), while clinical experience positively influenced them (PEOU: β=2.11, p<0.05). TAM construct analysis revealed that PEOU positively influenced PU (β=0.67, p<0.001), AT (β=0.31, p<0.01), and US (β=0.35, p<0.001). No significant correlation was found between US and BI (p=0.96). Discussion Findings suggest that PEOU significantly affects physicians’ behavioural intention to use alerts, with high patient volume and older age lowering acceptance due to alert fatigue. Adaptive, context-aware CDSS alerts can improve usability and align better with clinical workflows, enhancing efficiency in high-demand environments. Conclusion This study highlights the need for context-aware, frequency-optimised alert designs to enhance CDSS acceptance, improve user experience and streamline clinical workflows.
Methods: Single-centre outpatient study in northern Taiwan with 72 physicians completing a structured TAM-based questionnaire. Multiple regression analysis examined physician characteristics and relationships among TAM constructs.
Results: Age and patient volume negatively affected PU and PEOU, while clinical experience positively influenced them. PEOU positively influenced PU, AT, and US; US was not significantly correlated with BI (p=0.96).
Conclusions: Context-aware, frequency-optimised alert designs are needed to improve CDSS acceptance, user experience, and clinical workflow efficiency. Alert fatigue in older physicians and those with high patient volume is a key concern.

Authors: Herter, W.E.; Khuc, J.; Bonten, T.N.; ... Chavannes, N.H.
Source: Usability and Usefulness of Machine Learning–Based Clinical Decision Support Software in Primary Care: Survey of Users in a Prospective Observational Study
Abstract: Background: The successful implementation of decision support systems promises to enhance high-quality care. However, the successful implementation of a clinical decision support system (CDSS) depends on user acceptance and adoption. A machine learning (ML)–based CDSS to assist primary care professionals treating urinary tract infections (UTIs) was implemented, and usability and usefulness were assessed through a questionnaire. Objective: This study aimed to assess the system’s usability by examining users’ experiences with the software. A secondary goal was to assess users’ attitudes toward evidence-based practice and innovation in health care. Methods: In collaboration with the Netherlands Institute for Health Services Research (NIVEL) and Leiden University Medical Center (LUMC), Pacmed Ltd developed the CDSS. The cohort was mostly recruited at the care group level; practices within participating care groups were required to participate. Health insurers partly funded the research. Practitioners participated in the implementation study for 4 months. A survey based on the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) was sent to 263 general practitioners and assistants shortly after the implementation period. Furthermore, usage data were analyzed. Results: Of the 34 participating practices that used the software, 30 (88%) submitted at least one survey response, with a mean of 2.23 responses per practice (SD 1.43). The CDSS was used throughout the pilot period, and 31 practices continued using the tool, with 9% dropping out during the first 8 weeks. Sixty-seven percent of respondents trusted the tool’s output, and 73% found it understandable how the algorithm came to predictions. Sixty-five percent of respondents indicated that the information provided was useful in addition to the available guidelines, and 52% agreed that it supported their decision-making. However, many respondents were uncertain whether the tool improved patient care (46%) or patient outcomes (66%). Forty-eight percent of respondents found the software easy to integrate into their clinical workflow. Conclusions: The CDSS was perceived as trustworthy and easy to use. However, users were unable to determine whether the CDSS improved patient outcomes. In addition, the CDSS development could have benefited from including assistants as well as general practitioners more in the design phase of the software. Because assistants play an important role in UTI care, designing the software to better fit existing workflows may reduce the perceived time investment associated with using the tool. Finally, respondents reported strong motivation to contribute to further research in this field and indicated willingness to embrace change in health care delivery, which may also reflect selection bias in our sample.
Methods: Prospective observational implementation study of an ML-based CDSS for UTI care in primary care; 263 general practitioners and assistants received a UTAUT-based survey after 4 months, and usage data were analyzed.
Results: Of 34 participating practices, 30 (88%) responded; 31 practices continued using the tool and 9% dropped out in the first 8 weeks. Sixty-seven percent trusted the output, 65% found it useful, and 52% said it supported decision-making.
Conclusions: The CDSS was perceived as trustworthy and easy to use, but users could not determine whether it improved patient outcomes. The authors note that involving assistants more in design and better fitting workflows may reduce perceived time burden, and they caution that selection bias may be present.

Authors: Ji, M.; Genchev, G.Z.; Huang, H.; ... Yu, G.
Source: Evaluation framework for successful artificial intelligence–enabled clinical decision support systems: Mixed methods study
Abstract: Background: Clinical decision support systems are designed to utilize medical data, knowledge, and analysis engines and to generate patient-specific assessments or recommendations to health professionals in order to assist decision making. Artificial intelligence–enabled clinical decision support systems aid the decision-making process through an intelligent component. Well-defined evaluation methods are essential to ensure the seamless integration and contribution of these systems to clinical practice. Objective: The purpose of this study was to develop and validate a measurement instrument and test the interrelationships of evaluation variables for an artificial intelligence–enabled clinical decision support system evaluation framework. Methods: An artificial intelligence–enabled clinical decision support system evaluation framework consisting of 6 variables was developed. A Delphi process was conducted to develop the measurement instrument items. Cognitive interviews and pretesting were performed to refine the questions. Web-based survey response data were analyzed to remove irrelevant questions from the measurement instrument, to test dimensional structure, and to assess reliability and validity. The interrelationships of relevant variables were tested and verified using path analysis, and a 28-item measurement instrument was developed. Measurement instrument survey responses were collected from 156 respondents. Results: The Cronbach α of the measurement instrument was 0.963, and its content validity was 0.943. Values of average variance extracted ranged from 0.582 to 0.756, and values of the heterotrait-monotrait ratio ranged from 0.376 to 0.896. The final model had a good fit (χ<inf>26</inf><sup>2</sup>=36.984; P=.08; comparative fit index 0.991; goodness-of-fit index 0.957; root mean square error of approximation 0.052; standardized root mean square residual 0.028). Variables in the final model accounted for 89% of the variance in the user acceptance dimension. Conclusions: User acceptance is the central dimension of artificial intelligence–enabled clinical decision support system success. Acceptance was directly influenced by perceived ease of use, information quality, service quality, and perceived benefit. Acceptance was also indirectly influenced by system quality and information quality through perceived ease of use. User acceptance and perceived benefit were interrelated.
Methods: Mixed methods study developing and validating a 28-item AI-enabled clinical decision support evaluation instrument. Delphi process, cognitive interviews, pretesting, web-based survey (n=156), and path analysis were used.
Results: Cronbach α was 0.963 and content validity 0.943; AVE ranged 0.582-0.756 and HTMT 0.376-0.896. The final model fit was good and explained 89% of the variance in user acceptance.
Conclusions: User acceptance is the central dimension of AI-enabled clinical decision support system success. It was directly influenced by perceived ease of use, information quality, service quality, and perceived benefit; study is limited to an abstract-only report.

Authors: Zhu, J.; Wu, X.; Zhang, C.; ... Bian, X.
Source: AI-CDSS adoption among healthcare professionals: the influence of endowment-based autonomy threats and configuration preferences
Abstract: Objective: The rapid deployment of artificial intelligence-based clinical decision support systems (AI-CDSS) has outpaced current understanding of factors shaping healthcare professionals' adoption and resistance. This study examines how functional and endowment-based autonomy threats relate to resistance and intention to use AI-CDSS, and whether attitudes toward assistive versus replacement-oriented autonomous configurations differ across clinical scenarios. Methods: A cross-sectional survey was conducted among healthcare professionals at six hospitals across five Chinese cities that had deployed AI-CDSS, yielding 551 valid responses. The structural model integrated the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology, Technology Threat Avoidance Theory, and endowment effect theory, and was analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling and exploratory neural network analysis. A scenario-based repeated-measures analysis compared attitudes toward assistive versus replacement-oriented autonomous configurations across five clinical tasks. Results: Performance expectancy and social influence positively predicted behavioral intention, with social influence showing a stronger effect. Functional threats (to the diagnostic process and outcomes) and endowment-based threats (attachment to expertise and ownership loss) were significant predictors of resistance, which was associated with lower behavioral intention. Neural network analysis identified ownership loss as the most salient predictor of resistance. Healthcare professionals reported consistently more favorable attitudes toward assistive than toward replacement-oriented autonomous configurations across all tasks. Conclusions: Resistance to AI-CDSS reflects not only functional concerns about diagnostic processes and outcomes but also endowment-based threats related to expertise and ownership over clinical judgment. The consistent preference for assistive configurations suggests that preserving professional control is important for acceptance. Institutions and technology providers should prioritize autonomy-preserving design and clarify organizational expectations to support sustainable adoption and inform digital health policy. Public interest summary: Healthcare institutions are increasingly using artificial intelligence-based clinical decision support systems (AI-CDSS) to support clinical decision-making. This study surveyed 551 healthcare professionals across six hospitals in China to understand how they respond to AI-CDSS. Professionals expressed stronger intention to use AI-CDSS when they found it useful and when colleagues, supervisors, or institutional expectations supported its use. However, concerns about losing control over clinical decisions and feeling that professional expertise was being devalued increased resistance. Across five clinical situations, professionals consistently favored AI-CDSS that assisted their decisions over systems designed to perform tasks with minimal human involvement. These findings suggest that successful AI-CDSS implementation depends not only on technical usefulness, but also on designing systems that support, rather than replace, healthcare professionals' clinical authority and expertise.
Methods: Cross-sectional survey of 551 healthcare professionals from six Chinese hospitals using AI-CDSS, analyzed with PLS-SEM, exploratory neural network analysis, and scenario-based repeated-measures comparisons across five clinical tasks.
Results: Performance expectancy and social influence positively predicted behavioral intention; functional threats and endowment-based threats significantly increased resistance, and resistance reduced intention (β = -0.440, p < 0.001). Assistive AI-CDSS was rated more favorably than replacement-oriented autonomous AI-CDSS across all tasks (M = 3.70 vs 2.92; F(1,550)=358.54, p < 0.001).
Conclusions: AI-CDSS acceptance depends on preserving professional autonomy, expertise, and control, not just technical usefulness. Limitations include the cross-sectional, self-reported design and limited generalizability beyond hospitals in China.

Authors: Abousoliman, A.D.; Atta, M.H.R.; Hamed, H.M.
Journal: International Journal of Africa Nursing Sciences
Source: Acceptance of AI-based clinical decision support systems among registered nurses: psychological safety and the mediating role of professional identity in a cross-sectional study
Abstract: Background : AI-based clinical decision support systems are increasingly used to support clinical decision-making, patient safety, and evidence-based nursing practice. However, nurses' acceptance may be influenced by psychological and professional factors. Aim : This study examined the relationship between psychological safety and acceptance of AI-based clinical decision support systems among registered nurses and tested whether professional identity mediated this relationship. Methods : A descriptive cross-sectional correlational design was used. The study included 320 registered nurses from Kafr El-Sheikh University Hospitals, Egypt. Data were collected using Edmondson's Team Psychological Safety Scale, the Professional Identity in Nursing Scale 2.0, and an adapted modified UTAUT questionnaire. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, Pearson's correlation, multiple linear regression, and Hayes' PROCESS macro-Model 4. Results : Nurses reported moderate-to-high levels of psychological safety, professional identity, and acceptance. Acceptance was positively correlated with professional identity and psychological safety. Psychological safety was the strongest direct predictor of acceptance, whereas professional identity was not significant after controlling psychological safety. Professional identity did not mediate the relationship between psychological safety and acceptance. Conclusion : Psychological safety is central to nurses' acceptance of AI-based clinical decision support systems. Creating psychologically safe clinical environments may enhance nurses' engagement with AI-enabled decision support technologies.
Methods: Descriptive cross-sectional correlational survey of 320 registered nurses at Kafr El-Sheikh University Hospitals, Egypt. Data were collected with Arabic versions of the Psychological Safety Scale, Professional Identity in Nursing Scale 2.0, and adapted UTAUT questionnaire, and analyzed with correlations, multiple linear regression, and Hayes' PROCESS Model 4.
Results: Psychological safety, professional identity, and AI-based CDSS acceptance were moderate-to-high; acceptance correlated with professional identity (r=0.480, p<.01) and psychological safety (r=0.745, p<.01). Psychological safety was the strongest predictor of acceptance (β=0.741, p<.001); professional identity did not mediate the relationship.
Conclusions: Psychologically safe work environments are central to nurses' acceptance of AI-based CDSS. Professional identity was associated with acceptance but did not explain the psychological safety–acceptance link; the cross-sectional design limits causal inference.
